title: Understanding drama and performance
keyIdea: A play script is only part of a play. The director, designers and actors make choices that give the words their meaning on stage: an actor's tone, pauses and body language show the subtext, lighting sets the mood and tells the audience where to look, blocking places actors on stage, and the set tells the audience what kind of world they are in. Because each production makes different choices, two productions of the same script can interpret it differently, and both can still be faithful to the text if the words support them.

kid: A script gives the words. It does not tell you everything. Sarah says, "I'm fine." If she smiles and hugs Tom, she means it. If she pauses, looks down and turns away, she is hurt. The words stay the same. The meaning changes.
That hidden meaning is called subtext. Actors show it with their voice, their pauses and their body. Directors and designers add more: light, sound, the set and where people stand.
Stage directions use the actor's view. Stage left is the actor's left as they face the audience, so from your seat it is on the right. Downstage is the front, nearest you. Upstage is the back.

Two productions can stage one scene in very different ways. In one Macbeth, we see a glowing dagger. In another, the air is empty and his hand shakes. Both use the same words, but they suggest different things.
adult: This topic is about plays as performance, not just text. The English national curriculum for Key Stage 3 asks pupils to see how a play is brought to life on stage. It also asks how different staging can give different readings of the same play. In the US Common Core, grades 6 to 8 compare a script with a staged or filmed version. They judge how far it stays true to the script (RL.6.7 to RL.8.7).

Key terms. Subtext is the meaning under the words. Stage directions are the playwright's written notes. Blocking is where actors stand and move. Proxemics is the space between characters: far apart can show conflict. A naturalistic set copies a real place. A minimalist set uses very little. An expressionist set bends shapes and colours to show a character's mind.

Common mistakes. Pupils often treat the script as the whole play and only analyse the words. Many mix up stage left and stage right. These are given from the actor's view, facing the audience. Some think downstage means under the stage, but it is the front. Be careful, too, with calling a production wrong just because it is different. Ask instead: do the words support this choice?

In the lab your child directs one line to show two meanings and lights three scenes. They follow stage directions on a grid seen from the seats, match sets to a director's aim, and sort four stagings of Macbeth's dagger.

familyTip: Watch two different clips of the same scene from a play online (Shakespeare scenes are easy to find). Ask: what did each director or actor choose differently, and which version did you believe more? Why?

practice.prompt: An actor is told to move downstage. Where does she go?
choices: Towards the back of the stage
practice.hint: Old stages sloped down towards the seats.
practice.explain: Downstage is the part of the stage nearest the audience. Upstage is the back.

practice.prompt: A play has {s} scenes, each in a different place. A naturalistic production builds a full, detailed set for each one. How many set changes are needed between scenes?
practice.hint: The first set is already in place when the play starts. Count the changes after that.
practice.explain: The first scene starts on its set, so {s} scenes need {=s-1} changes. That is why many productions choose a minimalist set instead.

practice.prompt: The line is "I'm so happy for you." The actor says it through gritted teeth and walks away. What is the subtext?
choices: She is not happy for them
She is very happy for them
practice.hint: Do her voice and movement agree with her words?
practice.explain: Gritted teeth and walking away contradict the words, so the audience reads that she is not really happy.

practice.prompt: A scene has {n} lines in the script. The director cuts {c} of them to speed it up. How many lines are still spoken?
practice.hint: Start with all the lines in the script and take away the cuts.
practice.explain: {n} - {c} = {=n-c} lines are spoken. Cutting lines is one way a production can depart from the script, so ask whether the cuts change the meaning.

pool.prompt: An actor stands stage left. Where is she, seen from the audience?
pool.hint: Stage directions use the actor's view as they face the audience.
pool.explain: Stage left is the actor's left as they face the audience, so it is on the audience's right.

pool.prompt: A director wants a ghost scene to feel eerie. Which lighting fits best?
choices: Warm, bright light on the whole stage
pool.hint: Which light hides detail and feels unsettling?
pool.explain: Cold, dim blue light feels eerie and hides detail. Warm, bright light feels safe and open.

choices: The planned movement and position of actors on stage
pool.hint: It is about where actors stand and move.
pool.explain: Blocking is planned with the director: where each actor stands and moves, and when.

pool.prompt: In one production of Macbeth, the audience sees a glowing dagger. In another, the air is empty. What does the empty air suggest?
choices: The dagger is in his mind, a sign of guilt
pool.hint: Macbeth himself asks if it is "a dagger of the mind".
pool.explain: If only Macbeth sees it, the production suggests his guilty mind creates it, which the words "a dagger of the mind" support.

pool.prompt: Two productions of a play each make {c} choices about light, set and acting. If they make every choice differently, how many different choices are there altogether?
pool.hint: Each production has its own {c} choices. Add them.
pool.explain: {c} + {c} = {=2*c} different choices. The script is the same, but each set of choices gives a new interpretation.

pool.prompt: A director stages a play in a bare space with one chair. What kind of set is this?
pool.hint: Does it copy a real room, distort it, or use very little?
pool.explain: A minimalist set uses very little, which keeps the focus on the actors and allows quick scene changes.

pool.prompt: A production sets Romeo and Juliet in a modern city but keeps every word. What can you say about it?
choices: It departs from the setting but keeps the script's words
It is not Romeo and Juliet any more
It is exactly the same as the original
pool.hint: Separate what changed (where and when) from what stayed (the text).
pool.explain: The setting departs from Shakespeare's Verona, but the words are faithful. You can then judge whether the new setting helps the play's meaning.

pool.prompt: The lighting plan has {a} cues in Act 1 and {b} cues in Act 2. How many lighting cues does the operator run in the whole show?
pool.hint: A cue is one planned change of light. Add the two acts.
pool.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} cues. Each cue is a choice about mood or focus, so lighting is planned as carefully as the acting.
